title: Vikings Never Wore Horns? 0 Excavated Helmets Have Them. Who Put the Horns On?
description:
Your mental Viking probably has two horns; yet of all Viking Age helmets and fragments dug up, zero do. We follow the nine-piece iron helmet a farmer's son dug up in Ringerike, Norway, in 1943: "spectacles" over the eyes and nose, no horns. Scandinavia and Britain have only two near-complete Viking helmets. Hakonarmal (same century) and Heimskringla (c. 1225) mention many helmets, none horned. The truly horned Viksø helmets, found in a Danish bog in 1942 (66 years after Bayreuth 1876), date to about 900 BC per a 2021 study, some 1,700 years before the Viking Age. Horns were borrowed: Tacitus said the Germanic peoples rarely had helmets, yet in 1616 a geographer gave the Gauls' horns to the ancient Germans; 18th-century Vikings wore wings; in 1875 Carl Emil Doepler studied Tacitus; at the first complete Ring of the Nibelung in 1876 some warriors and attendants wore horns; no Viking was on stage. From the late 1870s, books switched: Erling the Bold's first eight illustrated editions show wings, the ninth (1890) horns. The Minnesota Vikings (first season 1961) painted horns on helmets.

Limits: the Viksø helmets' use is museums' and scholars' interpretation; Cosima Wagner and Montelius are quoted via Roberta Frank; "horns are impractical" is the Museum of the Viking Age's view; the horned helmet had no single inventor; the Tjele fragment's "134 years" is only on English Wikipedia. Sources below.

AI-generated illustrations; historical figures are unnamed cartoons, not likenesses; no modern researchers drawn.

Data as of 2026-10-20 (rewritten 2026-10-25 under new rules)

vk101.text: Picture a Viking, and he's probably wearing two horns.

vk102.text: Yet of the Viking helmets dug up, the number with horns is zero.

vk103.text: 1943, Ringerike, Norway. A farmer's son builds his parents a house.

vk104.text: On March 29, in the afternoon, he leveled a mound and hit a grave;

vk105.text: in it lay an iron helmet, broken into nine pieces.

vk106.text: Two days later, the local paper described it: no horns, but "spectacles."

vk107.text: That's not the oddest part. A year earlier, a spade in a Danish bog hit two helmets. These had horns.

vk108.text: Summer 1876, on a stage in Bayreuth, Germany, people put on horns. Who were they playing?

vk109.text: We follow that broken helmet from a 1,000-year-old grave to today's stadiums.

vk110.text: Why don't Viking helmets have horns? And who put the horns on?

vk201.text: The spectacles only made sense once it was rebuilt.

vk202.text: A round iron cap, a small spike on top;

vk203.text: over the eyes and nose, an iron frame, just like spectacles.

vk204.text: Iron rings line the rim. What hung there?

vk207.text: Around 1.5 kilograms, roughly what a modern soldier's helmet weighs.

vk208.text: It's named after that farm: the Gjermundbu helmet.

vk209.text: Surprisingly, the finds covered half the farmhouse living-room floor.

vk210.text: If it were yours, who'd you call first?

vk211.text: The next day, someone called the museum.

vk212.text: Three years into German rule, the museum was short-handed

vk213.text: and sent only a young researcher and a student. Arriving April 2, they finished in one day.

vk214.text: One day. Reading that, I felt nervous for them.

vk215.text: The same grave held a sword, two spears, two axes and riding gear;

vk216.text: by the researchers' count, even five or six horses, and sledges.

vk217.text: This grave: second half of the 900s.

vk218.text: Oddly, this helmet had been damaged on purpose.

vk219.text: The grave's two spears each pierced it;

vk220.text: part of the burial ritual, the museum says.

vk221.text: Costly: few warriors could afford one.

vk301.text: Two. In Scandinavia and Britain, only two near-complete ones exist, plus a few fragments.

vk303.text: Yarm, England, found while digging sewers in the 1950s;

vk304.text: a 2020 study placed it in the Viking Age; it too has spectacles over the face.

vk306.text: One in Denmark was found back in 1850,

vk307.text: but was taken for a saddle fitting for 134 years; only in 1984 was it recognized as a helmet's brows and nose guard.

vk308.text: Remember the zero from the start? It's these two plus these fragments, counted one by one.

vk309.text: Maybe you think: few finds don't mean none. So did writers back then ever give helmets horns?

vk310.text: We read a Norwegian court poem from that same century, Hakonarmal:

vk311.text: it has golden helmets and helmeted Valkyries, but no horns.

vk312.text: Then Heimskringla, a history written around 1225, mentions helmets dozens of times:

vk313.text: nose-guarded, gilded, painted with crosses, and not one horned.

vk314.text: Honestly, I was a bit let down here: not one exception.

vk315.text: Or were even helmets themselves rare?

vk316.text: Someone really argued that: a Norwegian neurosurgeon wrote in a 2000 paper that

vk318.text: That's his view alone; the museum only says few could afford one.

vk319.text: So who wore those two horned Danish helmets from the start?

vk401.text: Not Vikings. They went into the bog around 900 BC.

vk402.text: That date comes from a 2021 study that tested a bit of birch tar on one horn.

vk403.text: About 1,700 years before the Viking Age.

vk404.text: The spade from the start: a peat cutter's, 1942, Viksø, Zealand, Denmark,

vk405.text: and he heard a crunch beneath it.

vk406.text: So he took them for buried junk and set them aside.

vk407.text: Two grimy bits of bronze? You'd likely do the same.

vk408.text: Two near-identical bronze helmets: besides a pair of horns, they had eyes and a hooked beak.

vk409.text: The crown and horn tips may have held horsehair and feathers.

vk410.text: Horns that big: were they worn in battle?

vk411.text: Denmark's National Museum says no: they served religious rites;

vk412.text: part of a priest's costume, it says; only later were they offered up.

vk413.text: Such horns weren't rare in the Nordic Bronze Age: two small horned bronze men turned up in the 1700s,

vk414.text: and western Swedish rock art shows many horned men.

vk415.text: A Danish archaeologist studying them is blunter:

vk416.text: people tie them to Vikings, but actually, it's nonsense.

vk417.text: So did 19th-century people put horns on Vikings after seeing these?

vk501.text: At least not those two bog helmets. Remember that Bayreuth stage from the start?

vk502.text: These two surfaced 66 years after it.

vk503.text: What people could really see then: tiny men on helmet ornaments.

vk504.text: In 1870, four bronze dies turned up on Öland, Sweden, used to press helmet plates,

vk506.text: One shows an armed dancer with a pair of curved things on his head.

vk508.text: A Swedish archaeologist published the dies in 1872;

vk509.text: he wrote: it's a helmet with two raised parts, two bird necks turning toward each other.

vk510.text: He saw birds, not horns; it was later people who saw horns.

vk511.text: Scholar Roberta Frank says it mostly went the other way back then:

vk512.text: they pictured horned Vikings first, then saw horns in old objects.

vk513.text: Strange: the object is right there, yet what you see depends on what's already in your mind.

vk514.text: So where did the horned idea come from?

vk601.text: From older books. In AD 98, the Roman Tacitus wrote of the Germanic peoples:

vk602.text: barely one or two had helmets or hide caps.

vk603.text: You heard right: hardly any helmets, let alone horns.

vk604.text: Horns were borrowed from next door: another ancient historian said many Gaulish helmets had horns, making men look far taller.

vk605.text: In 1616, a geographer citing these old books put out an illustrated study of ancient Germany

vk606.text: that gave the ancient Germans horns.

vk607.text: But before this, what were painted Vikings wearing?

vk609.text: In 18th-century art, most Vikings wear winged helmets.

vk610.text: In 1825, Sweden published a very popular long poem, Frithiof's Saga;

vk611.text: its illustrated hero Frithiof wears an "eagle's helm."

vk612.text: In 1869, London saw a novel about a Norse sea-king: Erling the Bold;

vk613.text: and what's on its hero's head?

vk614.text: The book says atop his steel helmet rose spread hawk's wings, as if in flight.

vk615.text: In 1875, Wagner's costume designer Carl Emil Doepler set out to costume an opera;

vk616.text: he took it seriously: that spring he joined the Wagners at a play in Berlin, by a troupe famed for accurate costumes.

vk617.text: Then he opened Tacitus and its commentaries; waiting there were the horns passed down all along.

vk618.text: The story's great irony, I think: Doepler believed he was researching.

vk619.text: The next August, the curtain rose.

vk701.text: Picture yourself in that year's audience: onto the stage come gods, dwarfs, giants and heroes of myth;

vk702.text: on that stage from the start, not a single Viking.

vk703.text: August 1876: Bayreuth's Festival Theatre opens, and The Ring of the Nibelung is first staged complete.

vk704.text: Doepler put horns on some warriors and attendants;

vk705.text: yet the Valkyrie's helmet was white and winged.

vk706.text: Wagner's wife Cosima grumbled the costumes reminded her of "Indian chiefs."

vk707.text: That broke with tradition: until 1878, no illustrated Nibelungenlied had put horns on its characters.

vk708.text: But let me be clear: Doepler wasn't the first. Frank found an 1851 drawing

vk709.text: of the most famous Viking, Ragnar, in a custom goat-horned helmet; it's the only exception she found.

vk710.text: So how did the horns get from this stage onto Vikings' heads?

vk802.text: Remember Frithiof in his eagle's helm? By the late 1870s, a popular German book gave him horns.

vk803.text: Erling the Bold: all eight illustrated editions printed before 1880 show wings;

vk804.text: the ninth edition, in 1890, is the first with horns.

vk805.text: Surprisingly, an Icelandic saga put into English in 1861 did the same:

vk806.text: its first edition has no horned helmet; the 1900 frontispiece does.

vk807.text: Frank also notes: research suggests the term "Viking Age" was only coined around the 1870s;

vk808.text: she says no Viking Age, no horned Viking; the two grew up together.

vk810.text: Within 20 years, everywhere you can think of, ads, paintings, popular histories, children's books, Viking after Viking put on horns,

vk811.text: even on the menu of an 1895 cruise ship bound for Scandinavia.

vk812.text: Frank says that by the 1890s, horned Vikings were like the weather: everywhere.

vk813.text: When I read "like the weather," I genuinely laughed.

vk814.text: Yet the Vikings' homeland was slowest. Sweden's first homegrown horned Viking didn't appear until 1881;

vk815.text: Remember Heimskringla? In its 1899 Norwegian translation,

vk816.text: the Vikings drawn wear only conical helmets, row after boring row.

vk817.text: But Frank also says the horned helmet "had no single progenitor."

vk818.text: By 1900, the horns had become the Vikings' trademark.

vk901.text: They couldn't. In 1961, America's Minnesota Vikings played their first season,

vk902.text: with horns painted on the helmets' sides.

vk903.text: Later, for a Smithsonian Viking show, its shop could barely order Viking goods without horns.

vk904.text: Next museum gift shop you visit, look for a hornless helmet.

vk905.text: So, the iron helmet in nine pieces from the start: why no horns?

vk906.text: Nothing was ever missing; 19th-century people borrowed the horns from old books and the stage, and put them on Vikings.

vk908.text: Your first horned Viking: a cartoon, a ball game, or a storybook? Tell me in the comments.

vk909.text: This channel sticks to the record. To open files together, subscribe.
